newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr under siege as gains slip away.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr under siege as gains slip away.

text.p: The Australian dollar was holding just above 18-month lows late Wednesday having been slowly stripped of much of a 3/4 cent offshore rally.

The failure to press higher confirmed dealer suspicions the bounce was a mere short covering correction in a long term downtrend. Sentiment was soured by a mix of speculation about an official rate cut and weakness in commodity prices, all of which had dealers looking to sell into ther least sign of strength.
The only thing preventing a retest of US$0.7410 right now was the fact the market was already very short of dollars, and bears were hoping for fresh incentive from jobs data Thursday.

By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the unit had recoiled to US$0.7435/40 from an early US$0.7470 and a US$0.7493 high overnight. It was still up on Tuesday's late US$0.7418/23, but the failure to even hold former US$0.7440 support was seen as confirming the bearish outlook held by most chart watchers.
Tuesday's finish had been the currency's lowest since January 1996 and came after Prime Minister John Howard signalled the government's desire to see lower interest rates.
Analysts reckon that whether the RBA obliges depended mostly on what June quarter consumer price and wages data had to say about inflation when they were released on July 23 and 24.

The 40,300 fall in jobs recorded in May was such a shock the market had instantly begun to price in yet another rate cut but, perhaps peversely, analysts felt the June data would not be so relevant for policy unless wildly outside expectations.
Instead, most had decided that if the RBA was going to ease it would tag the move to low inflation and avoid the need to use disappointing economic growth as a justification.

Median estimates favour a rise in employment of around 40,250 for June, almost exactly correcting May's fall. The unemployment rate was seen edging down to a still high 8.7 percent from 8.8 percent the month before.

Analysts cautioned the dip in unemployment depended largely on the participation rate not recovering the fall suffered in May. For instance, if jobs rose 30,000 but the PR rate returned to April levels, the jobless rate would rise to 9.0 percent.

It would take an increase of more than 60,000 for the trend in employment growth to pick up even slightly and many suspected a jaded market would not be impressed by anything less than a 100,000 new jobs, a not unknown outcome but extremely rare.
A firm result was likely to prompt knee-jerk short covering and perhaps lift the dollar above 75 cents, although stiff resistance was expected at US$0.7530 and US$0.7550.

Equally, anything less than a 30,000 gain would be considered weak and an actual fall in employment would have the money market baying for an immediate cut in official rates and could see the dollar testing US$0.7410 again.

On the crosses the local currency lost early gains against the yen, to stand at 83.80/90 from 84.20/30, in the wake of figures showing Japan's current account surplus surged 155 percent in May to 906.8 billion yen.
The result was pretty much as the market expected but no less negative for that as it promised to keep trade tensions rumbling between Japan and the U.S.
The trade data also implied a net flow into the yen equal to the surplus, or in this case over 900 billion yen, which would tend to support the currency.

However, analysts noted that in the same period Japanese investors bought a total of 2.53 trillion yen of foreign bonds and stocks while offshore investors bought a net 941 billion yen of Japanese equity and debt.
That implied a net need by the Japanese to buy 1.59 trillion yen of foreign currency, quite a bit more than the demand for yen implied by the trade surplus.
This would normally act to restrain the yen but the market's political concerns were dominating at the moment and the U.S. dollar slipped to 112.75/80 yen after the data from an early 113.10/15.
In trade weighted terms the local currency ended at 56.8 from Tuesday's weak 56.5 close, but down on the opening 57.0.
